Glossary

The Odia and Sanskrit words used for the parts of a Kalinga temple, in plain English.

46 terms shown

No matching terms found. Try clearing your search or picking another letter.

Amla

The amla (also called amalaka) is a big, flattened, ribbed round part near the top of the tower. It looks like a giant amla fruit. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra: 'fluted oblate spheroid resembling an amalaka fruit'. Bose: 'a flattened spheroid, ribbed at the sides and resembling an enormous fruit of the amalaki'.

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Beki
  • Khapuri
  • Bhumi
Anuraha

On seven- and nine-strip walls, an extra strip called the anuraha sits right next to the middle raha. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra: 'projection next to the raha (central projection) in sapta-ratha and nava-ratha temples'.

See also

  • Paga
  • Raha
  • Anuratha
  • Saptaratha
  • Navaratha
Anuratha

On a five-strip (pancharatha) wall, the anuratha is the strip between the middle raha and the corner kanika. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra: 'projection next to the kanika-paga in pancha-ratha, sapta-ratha and nava-ratha temples'. On seven- and nine-strip walls the strip next to the raha is the anuraha, and the anuratha stays next to the kanika.

See also

  • Paga
  • Raha
  • Kanika
  • Anuraha
  • Pancharatha
Ayudha

The ayudha is the weapon or emblem of the temple's god, set at the top of the crown. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose: 'the ayudha or weapon of the deity to whom the temple is consecrated'. Mitra: 'sacred weapon or emblem'.

The emblem on top shows which god the temple is for. A Vishnu temple has a wheel (chakra); a Shiva temple has a trident or a linga. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: 'A Visnu temple is crowned by a chakra, a Siva temple either a Trisula or a Linga. The Sun temple has a lotus finial.'

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Kalasa
  • Dhvaja
Bada

The bada is the upright wall of the temple. It stands between the platform and the tower or roof. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose spells it 'bara'. It is not the same word as the 'bada' in bada deula, which means 'big'.

Early temples mostly have the three-part wall. The five-part wall is found in later temples. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) found that the Bhubaneswar temples he could date early 'have a bara composed of three elements', and that five parts appear 'only in the later temples'. Debala Mitra's ASI guide, describing Konark, says the wall has five divisions 'as in all Orissa temples'; that describes the fully developed temples. The dating rests on style.

Seen at

  • Parasuramesvara Temple
  • Konark Sun Temple

See also

  • Pabhaga
  • Jangha
  • Baranda
  • Trianga bada
  • Panchanga bada
  • Bada deula

See Bada in the Academy →

Bada deula

The main shrine is also called the bada deula, which means 'big temple'. This bada means 'big'. It is a different word from bada, the wall. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,4]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'bada deul literally big temple, meaning the sanctuary'; the same glossary lists 'bada ... wall' as a separate entry. Kramrisch writes 'Bara Deul'.

See also

  • Deula
  • Bada
  • Vimana
Bandhana

The bandhana is a band of mouldings that divides the jangha into a lower and an upper part. Its name means 'that which binds'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'That which binds; set of mouldings between janghas'; in his text, 'the bandhana or the bond'.

See also

  • Jangha
  • Tala jangha
  • Upara jangha
  • Panchanga bada
Baranda

The baranda is the set of mouldings that crowns the top of the wall, just below the tower or roof. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Also spelled varanda (Mitra, Behera).

See also

  • Bada
  • Upara jangha
  • Gandi
Beki

The beki is the narrow round neck just above the tower. The word means 'neck' or 'throat'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose calls it 'the throat'; Debala Mitra 'neck'. Behera: it 'separates the square gandi from the circular crowning elements'.

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Amla
  • Gandi
Bhogamandapa

The bhogamandapa is the hall of offering. It usually stands in front of the dance hall. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,5]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown and K.S. Behera also call it 'the refectory hall of a temple', a dining hall. At Konark the detached hall in front is named both ways: Mitra says it 'is generally believed to be a nata-mandapa' and 'is also known as the bhoga-mandapa'.

Seen at

  • Lingaraja Temple
  • Jagannath Temple, Puri

See also

  • Natamandira
  • Jagamohana

See Bhogamandapa in the Academy →

Bhumi

On a rekha tower, the corner strips are divided into storeys called bhumis. A small amla, the bhumi-amla, marks the top of each storey. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose calls the bhumis 'planes', Behera 'levels'. Bose: each is 'surmounted by a miniature amla, called the bhumi-amla'.

See also

  • Kanika
  • Amla
  • Gandi
Deula

Deula is the local word for a temple. Used alone, it often means just the main shrine with its tower. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,5]

For curious grown-ups

Debala Mitra's ASI guide: 'general name for a temple as a whole; when used singly, it refers to the sanctuary'. Percy Brown (1959) says the same. Spellings vary: deul (Mitra, Brown), deula (Behera).

Odisha's temples come in three main types: rekha, pidha and khakhara. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Debala Mitra sorts Bhubaneswar's temples into 'Rekha, Pidha and Khakhara orders'. K.S. Behera says the local silpa texts 'mention three types of structures'. N.K. Bose (1932) counts four types in Orissa, adding the rare Gauriya, and calls the pidha type 'Bhadra'.

A typical Odisha temple joins two types. A rekha tower rises over the shrine, and a pidha hall stands in front of it. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,4,5]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown: the deul and the jagamohan 'combined constitute the essentials of the Orissan temple type'. Mitra's example is Konark.

From bottom to top, a temple has four parts: the pista (platform), bada (wall), gandi (tower or roof) and mastaka (crown). Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) names the four parts and says 'mastaka' is a name coined for convenience. K.S. Behera also calls the crown 'shira'. Percy Brown (1959) uses other names for the tower's parts. The platform is spelled pista (Bose, Brown), pishta (Mitra) or pitha (Behera).

Many part names come from the human body, such as foot, leg, trunk, throat and head. Scholars say the temple was pictured as a body. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): 'the Rekha temple has been likened to the human body'. Debala Mitra: naming parts after human limbs 'suggests that temples were likened to the human body'. K.S. Behera goes further: the craftsmen 'considered the temple as the body of the Cosmic Being'.

See also

  • Rekha deula
  • Pidha deula
  • Khakhara deula
  • Bada deula
  • Vimana
Dhvaja

A flag, the dhvaja, is raised at the very top of the temple. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: 'The dhvaja or banner is placed at the pinnacle of the temple.'

See also

  • Ayudha
  • Mastaka
Gandi

The gandi is the main body of the tower or roof, above the wall. The word means 'trunk', as in the trunk of a body. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'literally trunk; curvilinear spire or pyramidal roof above bada and below the mastaka'. Percy Brown (1959) calls the tall middle part of the tower the 'chhapra' instead.

Seen at

  • Lingaraja Temple
  • Mukteshvara Temple

See also

  • Bada
  • Mastaka
  • Bhumi
  • Pidha

See Gandi in the Academy →

Ghanta

On a pidha roof, the crown has a big bell-shaped part called the ghanta, also called sri. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose: 'an enormous ribbed structure shaped like a bell'. Mitra: 'bell-shaped member in the finial of a pidha temple; it is also called sri'.

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Pidha deula
  • Beki
Jagamohana

The jagamohana is the hall in front of the main shrine, where worshippers gather. It usually has a pidha (stepped) roof. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'hall in front of a sanctuary, usually in a pidha temple'. The earliest halls did not have a stepped roof yet.

The word jagamohana is explained as 'that which pleases the whole world'. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Jagamohan — That which pleases the whole world; that which is most pleasing'.

Seen at

  • Konark Sun Temple
  • Lingaraja Temple
  • Mukteshvara Temple
  • Parasuramesvara Temple
  • Jagannath Temple, Puri

See also

  • Pidha deula
  • Natamandira
  • Bhogamandapa

See Jagamohana in the Academy →

Jangha

The jangha is the tall, upright face of the wall, above the foot mouldings. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

Jangha is a body word for part of the leg. It has been translated both as 'shin' and as 'thigh'. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) translates jangha as 'shin'. Debala Mitra (ASI) and K.S. Behera translate it as 'thigh'. They agree on which part of the wall it is.

See also

  • Bada
  • Tala jangha
  • Upara jangha
  • Bandhana
Kalasa

The kalasa is a part shaped like a water-pot, set on top of the khapuri. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera says the kalasa 'was sometimes made of gold'; Mitra records a copper kalasa at Konark.

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Khapuri
  • Ayudha
  • Kumbha
Kani

The kani is a moulding shaped like a letter V lying on its side. It is one of the mouldings in the foot of the wall. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Moulding of the shape of a V placed sideways'. The scan reads the headword as 'Kant'; its place between Kalasa and Kanika and the index entry 'kani p.' show it is kani.

See also

  • Pabhaga
  • Pata
Kanika

The kanika is the corner paga, the outermost strip at each corner of the temple. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Also called kanika-paga (Mitra, Behera) or kanyasa (Bose).

See also

  • Paga
  • Anuratha
  • Bhumi
Khakhara deula

A khakhara deula has an oblong (rectangular) plan. Its roof is long and rounded on top, like half a barrel lying on its side. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): the ground plan of the khakhara 'is rectangular'. K.S. Behera: 'oblong bada and semi-cylindrical roof'. Mitra's ASI guide calls the roofs of its carved models 'wagon-vaulted'.

Two khakhara temples in Bhubaneswar are the Vaital Deul and the small Gauri temple. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [2,6]

The name khakhara comes from the kakharu, a kind of pumpkin-gourd. The temple's long, rounded roof looks a little like it. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [7]

For curious grown-ups

Debala Mitra (1960): the name is 'due to the faint resemblance of the barrel-vaulted elongated roof of its temples with a variety of pumpkin-gourd, called kakharu in Oriya'. She links the local name vaitalu for this gourd with the name of the Vaital Deul.

This roof shape may copy very old halls, whose rounded roofs rested on timber or bent bamboo. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [7]

For curious grown-ups

Debala Mitra (1960): the roof 'is a modified survival of the primitive halls with a semi-cylindrical roof resting on a framework of timber or bent split bamboos (in the case of a thatched roof)'.

Khakhara temples are often linked with the worship of goddesses. But goddesses are also found in temples of other types, and experts do not all agree about the Vaital Deul. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [3,5,7]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera (2005): the khakhara temple is 'used for Devi worship'. Debala Mitra (1960): the available evidence 'indicates that temples of this Order in Orissa belonged to the Sakta cult, though the converse is not true', as goddesses also sit in rekha temples such as the Mohini and Chitrakarini. Percy Brown (1959) calls the Vaital Deul 'a Siva temple of the Orissan group'.

Full khakhara temples are rare. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): the type 'is limited to six examples in Bhubaneswar', but its miniatures are very common as decoration.

See also

  • Khakhara-mundi
  • Rekha deula
  • Pidha deula
Khakhara-mundi

A khakhara-mundi is a small carved model of a khakhara temple. Many temple walls are decorated with them. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'miniature representation of a khakhara temple as an ornamental motif'. Bose (1932): such miniatures 'were very extensively employed as a decorative motif'. Konark's walls have many (Mitra, scan leaves 46 and 53).

Seen at

  • Konark Sun Temple

See also

  • Khakhara deula
Khapuri

The khapuri is a flattish, bell-shaped cap above the amla. Its name means 'skull'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

See also

  • Mastaka
  • Amla
  • Kalasa
Kumbha

The kumbha is one of the mouldings in the foot of the wall. It is shaped like a water-pot, and kumbha means 'water-pot'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose's glossary: 'Kumbha — Water-pot; similar moulding used in pabhaga'. Behera's glossary: 'water pot; pitcher-shaped moulding of the pabhaga'.

See also

  • Pabhaga
  • Kalasa
Mastaka

The mastaka is the crown: the stack of round parts on top of the tower. The word means 'head'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'head; crowning elements above the gandi'. Bose (1932): its elements 'are all circular in cross-section'.

The name mastaka is modern. It was made up to make the crown easier to talk about. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): 'The mastaka (a name which has been coined for the sake of convenience)'. Debala Mitra and K.S. Behera use it as the standard term; Behera also gives 'shira'.

See also

  • Beki
  • Amla
  • Khapuri
  • Kalasa
  • Ayudha
  • Ghanta
  • Gandi
Natamandira

The natamandira is the dance hall. In large temples it stands in front of the jagamohana. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,5]

For curious grown-ups

Names vary: Nat Mandir (Brown), nata mandapa (Mitra), Nata-mandira (Behera). Mitra's glossary calls it a 'festive hall'; her Lingaraja text, Brown and Behera say 'dancing hall'.

In the largest temples, four buildings stand in one straight line: deula, jagamohana, natamandira and bhogamandapa. The two front halls were often added later. The Lingaraja Temple and the Jagannath Temple in Puri both have all four. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,5]

For curious grown-ups

Debala Mitra: the Lingaraja 'consists of the customary four structures', 'disposed on the same axis but do not necessarily belong to the same period'; at Puri the nata and bhoga-mandapas are 'later additions'. Percy Brown: the extra halls 'were added to the front of the assembly hall'.

Seen at

  • Lingaraja Temple
  • Jagannath Temple, Puri
  • Konark Sun Temple

See also

  • Jagamohana
  • Bhogamandapa

See Natamandira in the Academy →

Navaratha

A navaratha temple has nine pagas on each side. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

See also

  • Paga
  • Saptaratha
  • Anuraha
Pabhaga

The pabhaga is the 'foot' of the wall. It is a stack of three to five shaped stone bands, called mouldings, at the very bottom. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): 'Division corresponding to the foot; set of three, four or five mouldings at the base of a temple'.

Often the foot has five mouldings, named khura, kumbha, pata, kani and basanta. Some temples have only three or four. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [2,3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: the pabhaga 'is composed of mouldings called khura, kumbha, pata, kani and basanta'. One passage in Bose (1932) puts 'kalasa' in place of kumbha; his glossary says kalasa can '(rarely)' mean the kumbha moulding.

Seen at

  • Parasuramesvara Temple

See also

  • Bada
  • Kumbha
  • Pata
  • Kani
  • Jangha

See Pabhaga in the Academy →

Paga

A paga (also called a ratha) is an upright strip of the outer wall that steps forward. Inside, the walls are usually kept plain. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra: projections 'known in Orissan Silpa-sastras or architectural canons as rathas or pagas'. Bose: the inner walls 'are kept rigorously plain', though Mitra notes mouldings on the inner walls of Konark's porch.

See also

  • Raha
  • Kanika
  • Anuratha
  • Anuraha
  • Triratha
  • Pancharatha
Panchanga bada

A panchanga bada is a wall in five parts: pabhaga, tala jangha, bandhana, upara jangha and baranda. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

Bose writes 'pancha-anga'.

See also

  • Trianga bada
  • Bada
  • Bandhana
Pancharatha

A pancharatha temple has five pagas on each side. The middle strip is stepped forward a second time. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

Seen at

  • Lingaraja Temple
  • Mukteshvara Temple
  • Jagannath Temple, Puri

See also

  • Paga
  • Triratha
  • Saptaratha
  • Anuratha
Pata

The pata is a moulding with a square edge. It is used in the foot of the wall and in other bands of mouldings. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose's glossary (1932): 'Pata — Moulding with a square edge.'

See also

  • Pabhaga
  • Kani
  • Bandhana
Pidha

A pidha is one flat, jutting layer of a pidha roof. The word means a flat wooden seat. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

See also

  • Pidha deula
  • Potala
Pidha deula

A pidha deula has a roof like a stepped pyramid. It is built from flat layers, called pidhas, that get smaller as they rise. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) calls this type 'Bhadra'. K.S. Behera: the uppermost pidha is generally 'half the size of the lowest one'.

The pidha form is mostly used for a temple's halls: the jagamohana, the dance hall and the hall of offerings. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,6]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra's ASI glossary: 'usually limited to the jagamohana, bhoga-mandapa and nata-mandapa in Orissa'.

The stepped pidha roof came later. In the earliest temples, the hall in front had a lower, flatter roof. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3,6]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: in the earlier phase the jagamohana 'was distinguished by a flat roof'. K.C. Panigrahi: the early porch is 'a low mandapa', and the pidha form first appears as the porch of the Mukteshvara.

The pidha hall in front of the shrine is also called a bhadra deula, or a mukhasala, which means 'front hall'. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose (1932): the Bhadra is also called the Mukhasala, 'the building which is placed towards the face or front of the Rekha'. Mitra glosses bhadra deul as 'auspicious temple'.

Seen at

  • Konark Sun Temple
  • Mukteshvara Temple

See also

  • Pidha
  • Potala
  • Jagamohana
  • Rekha deula
Pista

The pista is the platform or base that a temple stands on. Not every temple has one. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,5]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): the pista 'does not form an essential part of the temple proper'; the Lingaraja has none. Spellings: pista (Bose, Brown), pishta (Mitra), pitha (Behera).

Seen at

  • Konark Sun Temple

See also

  • Bada
  • Deula

See Pista in the Academy →

Potala

The pidhas are often grouped into tiers. Each tier is called a potala. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: the gap between two potalas 'is known as kanti'.

See also

  • Pidha
  • Pidha deula
Raha

The raha is the middle paga on each side of the temple. It sticks out the furthest. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Bose records a second name for it: go-ratha or madhya-ratha. Behera: the side-shrine gods (parsvadevatas) sit in its niche.

See also

  • Paga
  • Anuraha
  • Kanika
Rekha deula

A rekha deula has a tall, curved tower. The tower rises almost straight at first, then curves inward more and more near the top. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) compares the outline to 'a tall bamboo-post which has been slightly bent towards the top by a rope'. Mitra's ASI glossary: 'a curvilinear tower which presents the appearance of a continuous line'.

The rekha form is usually used for the main shrine, the sanctuary. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3,4]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: 'usually limited to the main temple'. Stella Kramrisch calls the sanctuary the 'Rekha or Bara Deul'. Mitra's example is Konark, whose rekha tower has fallen.

Seen at

  • Konark Sun Temple
  • Jagannath Temple, Puri
  • Mukteshvara Temple

See also

  • Pidha deula
  • Gandi
  • Deula
Saptaratha

A saptaratha temple has seven pagas on each side. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

See also

  • Paga
  • Pancharatha
  • Navaratha
  • Anuraha
Silpa sastra

The silpa sastras are Odisha's traditional building manuals. Temple builders followed them. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: 'In the construction of temples, Silpasastra texts are followed.' Debala Mitra calls them 'Orissan Silpa-sastras or architectural canons'.

The names rekha, pidha and khakhara are found in these manuals. There, the pidha type is also called bhadra. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3,6]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): 'in the silpasastras, there are specifications of 55 Rekha, 6 Bhadra and 3 Khakhara temples'. K.C. Panigrahi: 'In the canons of Orissan architecture it is known as the Pidha or Bhadra type'. K.S. Behera: the local texts 'mention three types of structures, rekha, pidha and khakara'.

See also

  • Deula
  • Rekha deula
  • Pidha deula
  • Khakhara deula
Tala jangha

The tala jangha is the lower jangha, between the pabhaga and the bandhana. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

See also

  • Jangha
  • Upara jangha
  • Bandhana
Torana

A torana is a gateway with an arch that stands on its own. The Mukteshvara Temple in Bhubaneswar has one in front: a round arch on two pillars. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [5,6]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown: 'This detached portal consists of two pillars supporting a round arch within a semi-circular shaped pediment'. K.C. Panigrahi: no torana is found at any other existing temple in Bhubaneswar; the remains of an earlier one were dug up at Dola-mandapa.

Seen at

  • Mukteshvara Temple

See also

  • Jagamohana

See Torana in the Academy →

Trianga bada

A trianga bada is a wall in three parts: the foot (pabhaga), the tall middle (jangha) and the top band (baranda). Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): the early temples 'have a bara composed of three elements, viz. pabhaga, jangha and baranda'.

Trianga means 'three-part'. It is a modern name, not an old builders' word. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932): 'The tri-anga (a name coined to denote a three-segmented) bara'.

Early temples mostly have the three-part wall. The five-part wall is found in later temples. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

N.K. Bose (1932) found that the Bhubaneswar temples he could date early 'have a bara composed of three elements', and that five parts appear 'only in the later temples'. Debala Mitra's ASI guide, describing Konark, says the wall has five divisions 'as in all Orissa temples'; that describes the fully developed temples. The dating rests on style.

See also

  • Panchanga bada
  • Bada
Triratha

A triratha temple has three pagas on each side: a raha in the middle and a kanika at each corner. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2]

Seen at

  • Parasuramesvara Temple

See also

  • Paga
  • Pancharatha
  • Raha
  • Kanika
Upara jangha

The upara jangha is the upper jangha, between the bandhana and the baranda. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Spellings: upara jangha (Mitra), upar jangha (Bose).

  • Tala jangha

Vimana

The main shrine with its tower is also called the vimana. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3,5]

For curious grown-ups

K.S. Behera: 'The main temple or the Vimana (also called deula)'. Percy Brown: deul can mean 'the sanctuary only, such as the cella and its tower, the vimana'.
